mood: three lines rigged and baited for dawn, a peg for the second corner
nails: a keg of a few thousand in three lengths; ten short ones used, one bent and drawn
pantry: food bundle from his maker: most of a loaf less four heels, a wheel of cheese less five wedges, a little under a ring of smoked sausage, a sack of oats less two fists, a sack of dried beans, most of a bag of nuts less a handful, most of a string of dried apples less two, a crock of salt less a pinch, a jar of honey; about five days left

plan.doing: sitting by his fire with his hands held out to it, looking across the water
plan.goal: let the day settle while the fire burns

plan.doing: picking worms out of the damp leaves under the dead limb by firelight
plan.goal: have bait ready tonight so all three lines go in at first light without digging

plan.doing: carving a peg for the second sill corner by his fire
plan.goal: lock the second corner of the sill frame the way the first one is locked

plan.doing: sitting by his fire with his hands held out to it, listening
plan.goal: let the fire warm him through and wind down before bed

threads.name: Getting out
threads.summary: Arrived at night, made camp east of the creek, to find the west his people say isn't there. Compass: a hammered steel sliver, magnetized with forty strokes of the stone his maker left (with honey) in the basket on the stump across the creek; his maker also offered a board and pencil for mapping. A shadow stick gave a true east-west line; the sliver lies square across it, but his first 'north' notch was on the south end, so he filed a new one and scratched an infinity mark by the east pebble. Read that a needle floated on cork in still water swings less; floated it on a disc of stalk pith in a tin lid and it settles in four swings, but drifts to the rim and sticks. Wings: notched joints and two-ply stalk cord; snapped the long side spar at its groove but it split a thumb past it, so now that side is a thumb short the other way. Lantern oil is low; one lit at a time. His maker says he set the stage and the rest, food included, is Gage's to work out. Filled the lid until the water domed above the rim: the float sits centered, but one spilled drop and it runs back to the edge. His maker left a quart of lamp oil and a bundle of bread, cheese, jerky and dried apple in the basket, with a note that feeding himself is still his job. Read that a float the water wets slides uphill along the curve of the water, so it runs to a wall the water climbs; a float the water doesn't wet gets pushed off it. That's why the brim-full lid worked. Rubbed lamp oil into the pith float: it stays off the rim now but the oil film makes it drag. Read that a split spar is bound with tight turns past both ends of the crack; twisted fresh stalk cord and whipped the side spar, crack closed to a hairline, still a thumb short. Hung his weight on it: held but bowed, crack opened under load, turns crept; not glide-worthy. Read that compasses sit the needle in liquid on purpose so it stops swinging; the drag is wanted. Rinsed the lid with sand; in clean water the oiled float settles in two and a half swings, but bumps still move it. Read a page asking whether metal near a compass throws it off; slid the wrench toward the lid and the needle turned to follow it at a hand's width. Moved the vise to the far end of the bench (sits on two bolts, rocks a little) and keeps the wrench on the crate: knocked five times, the needle came back to the same line every time. Wind is still a problem. Read that boat builders fix a cracked spar by sistering a second piece alongside, past both ends of the crack. Pulled a forearm-long stick from the scrap pile and lashed it along the side spar bow side out; the ends bite but the middle leaves a fingernail gap. Ate a third of the loaf and some cheese, rationing the rest. Hung off the splinted spar: half the bow, but the crack opened in the middle where the gap was. Six middle turns cranked tight closed the gap; second hang barely bowed and the crack stayed shut, but the near-end turns slid a finger on the slick bark. Needs a notch for the lashing to bite. Filed three notches across the splint's near end and lashed it back on with the last cord, seven turns. Third hang: the turns stayed put, but something at the root joint ticked once. At night the float creeps a hair off the line with no wind; maybe warm air off the lit lantern. Half the food bundle left. Found an oil-stained square of canvas in the scrap pile and draped it over the lid: the float creeps less shaded, but lifting the cloth to look stirs the air again; a cover needs a window. Stripped a dozen stalks by lantern glow and twisted two arm-lengths of cord for the eighth turn. Laid the eighth turn into the splint's last notch, tight; the hang waits for daylight. Ate half the jerky. Held the honey jar to the lantern: besides the lantern globes it's his only clear glass, too small to cover the lid, but a window needn't be big. Last look under the canvas: four swings, then the same creep. Searched the scrap pile for anything clear and found none; the honey jar's bottom may have to become the window. Turned in early, worn out. Woke rested, ate a heel of bread and some cheese. Daylight hang on the eight-turn splint: crack stayed shut, turns didn't creep, but the root joint ticked twice and rocks a hair in its lashing. Read that a lashing needs frapping turns between the poles to cinch the wraps; his root joint has none. Went for stalks to twist more cord. Twisted four arm-lengths of cord and wound six frapping turns at the root joint: the rock stopped. First hang silent; on the second the top frap sawed on the sharp notch edge and a ply parted. Read that sailors parcel rope with cloth strips and round off hard edges. Read to parcel with the lay, strips overlapping like shingles. Ate a third of the remaining loaf and four apple rings. Unwound the parted frap and filed the notch lip round in twelve strokes. Tore two strips off the lid's shade canvas, parceled the root joint and laid a fresh frap over it; not hung on yet. Read that a bottle can be cut by burning an oil-soaked string around it and plunging it in cold water; the edge comes out sharp. Ate a third of the honey off a finger to start emptying the jar and twisted a thin cord for the cut. Test-burned a hand of thin cord soaked in lamp oil around a spar stick: it smoked and went out at the knot two-thirds around, costing a thimble of oil. Read to wind three to five turns, use fast fuel and keep the bottle turning; gathered another armful of stalks for about two arm-lengths of finer cord. Finished two arm-lengths of thin cord. Hung off the wing root joint after it sat: silent twice, but on a bounce the stand's left leg kicked out and the frame dropped a hand; the stand needs bracing. Read that string-cutters use thin quick fuels; lamp oil needs a wick, so the cord must soak through. Ate the last honey on bread; the jar is empty. Read that swing sets stop swaying with diagonal triangles and anchors driven in at each leg. Pulled a forearm-long stick from the scrap pile, drove it in beside the stand's left leg (moved it a thumb off a root) and lashed the leg to it with one of the two arm-lengths of thin cord, leaving only one for the jar. Three hangs and a bounce: the leg stays, the lashing creaks but holds; the right leg is still unbraced. Read that a slanted brace takes a diagonal lashing at each end (timber hitch around both poles, wraps both ways, then frapping), so two lashings. Stripped stalks and twisted an arm-length and a half of thin cord: two and a half in all, enough for the jar cut or one end of a brace, not both; the brace goes first. Dug a straight, wrist-thin stick out of the scrap pile for the brace, about an arm too short; a sheet of tin slid off the pile with a clatter. Read the rule of thumb of about three feet of rope per inch of combined pole thickness: roughly two arm-lengths per lashing for his poles. Ate the last jerky and apple rings; a heel of bread and a bit of cheese left, then the acorn tin. Lashed the top of the short, steep brace to the right leg with a diagonal lashing; half an arm-length of cord left and the brace's foot only rests on the dirt. Drove a pointed stub at the brace foot; round on round, the foot rolled off when he leaned. Read about the bird's mouth, a V cut so a rafter sits over its beam; a brace that only pushes needs no cord at its foot. Lit the bench lantern at sundown, oil can still better than half. Filed a V a thumb deep into the brace foot and sat it over the stake: it holds a lean, but one side is steeper and it twists a hair; not hung yet. Filed the steep face of the V even; no twist. Hanging on the braced stand: silent twice, but on a bounce the stake under the brace leaned a finger in the soft dirt; the joint holds, the ground doesn't. Ate the last heel of bread and cheese; the bundle is empty, so it's the acorn tin now. Knocked the brace stake deeper with a stone: half a hand, then it hit root or rock. Three bounces on the frame: the stake held, the brace stayed seated, the splint creaked but held. Twisted the last stripped fiber into one arm-length of two-ply; the jar cut wants two. Snapped an armful of stalks by lantern and twisted half an arm-length more; some were too green and tore short. Moved the lantern to the wing stand and the float still crept a hair at night: not the lantern's heat, or not only. Then saw the lid's dome had sunk a hair under the rim over the evening; poured it brimming again and the float went back to center in three swings. The creep is the water drying down, so the lid needs a cover. Twisted another quarter arm of cord: one and three-quarters of the two the jar cut needs. Finished the second arm-length: two arm-lengths of two-ply wrap the honey jar's shoulder six times with a hand to spare, enough for a second try. The bottom third of honey has to go first. Ate the last of the honey and washed the jar clear in the shallows by lantern; one small bubble in the glass. Topped the lid up from it when the dome sank again. Soaked the cord in a thimble of oil and wrapped three turns around the jar's shoulder; the burn waits for first light. Before bed the float sat on center in the fresh dome; hanging on the wing frame, the outer turn of the side-spar splint slid a finger toward the joint, so it gets retied by daylight. In the morning the dome had sunk overnight and the float sat on the rim; topped it from the jar. Read that burn cracks often run off the line and slower, more even heat may help, so he turned the jar as the oiled cord burned over the shallows. Quenched it: the crack ran two-thirds round on the line, then wandered down toward the bubble. The top came off and left a clear cup with a thumb-long tooth on the rim; it needs grinding flat before it can cover the lid. Read that a cut rim is lapped flat in figure-eights on wet grit over a flat plate until it's frosted all round; a flat creek stone and shallows sand may do, once the tooth is off. Unwound the splint's outer turn, relaid it hard and added a ninth turn with the last half arm-length of cord. Two full-weight hangs: the frame groaned, but the turn didn't creep and the crack stayed shut. No cord left. Read to bring a cut rim down on coarse wet grit first, light pressure, turning the glass every few circles, palm off the sharp side; the tooth goes first. Pulled an armful of stalks down the same gap and twisted two arm-lengths of cord. Dug coarse sand from under the shallows stones and ground the tooth down by half in figure-eights, but a sliver chipped off the outside of the rim. Read that the sharp edge needs a small bevel (an arris) first or it chips. The cup still rocks over the lid. Ground a small bevel round the outside of the rim, light strokes, turning the cup; the edge frosted over and nothing more chipped. Read that a rim is lapped face down on grit on something dead flat, in circles with even pressure, until it's frosted all round; shiny spots are low spots. Lapped the cup on wet sand on the flattest shallows stone: the tooth stub is gone, but two shiny spots remain opposite it. Read that hand lapping is usually done in figure-eights; switched from circles to figure-eights, turning the cup a quarter every ten strokes. One shiny spot frosted over and the other shrank by half, but the middle of his lapping stone is wearing low too. Read that two plates rubbed together only come out as a matching dome and dish; three rubbed in turns come out flat. Picked a hand-wide dark slab from the shallows that rocks least. Rubbing it face to face on the lapping stone with wet sand, the slab's middle is settling into the hollow: the dome and dish. Needs a third stone. Picked a pale gray third stone with a lump near one edge. Read that people flattening whetstones draw a pencil grid on the face and lap until all the lines go at once; marked the pale stone with lantern soot instead. Rubbed it face down on the hollow lapping stone with wet sand: after forty strokes the soot was gone only off the lump and one corner. His maker sent a message: paper, a pencil and a glass dome in the basket at the stump. Read that a map is paced distances and compass directions written down; counted sixty-one paces from the stepping stones to the stump. Set the dome over the lid: in a steady south breeze the float does not shiver. But at sundown the inside fogged with beads off the warm water, and lifting it to wipe let cold air knock the float off line. The honey-jar window and the stone lapping can wait. By lantern, drew the first lines on the map sheet: camp, the creek and stepping stones, the stalks, the oak, sixty-one paces to the stump, an x where the smoke rises; the whole west of the sheet blank. Propped the dome on a pebble to let the fog out; it clears slowly from the gap side. By full dark the pebble-propped dome had cleared except a rim on the far side, the sliver plain on its north notch; the air was still, so the wind question waits. With one lantern lit half the bench is in shadow; dug a hand-wide piece of tin out of the scrap pile to stand behind it as a reflector, but it's folded at a corner and dented like a spoon, so it wants hammering flat in daylight. Drew a north arrow on the map off the needle, crescent-and-dot at the head and an infinity mark for east; the west end of the arrow is unmarked like the compasses back home, and the west half of the sheet is blank past sixty-one paces. Lashed the rear side-spar joint: six turns, cord ran out before a frapping turn. Filed a test notch round a scrap spar end to see if notched turns can make up for the rear joint's missing seventh. Decided that in daylight he'll take the sheet and pencil past the stump and keep pacing west until something stops him. Out of cord, wound the paper roll's twine into the notch on the scrap spar: the turns didn't slide, but the second hang split the spar from the bottom of the notch, so a notch on the real spar must be no deeper than the cord. Under the dome the compass water still humps over the rim after hours. Went to bed early for the daylight walk west. At dawn the dome was beaded inside but the float sat on its north notch and the water was still humped over the rim. Realized the compass can't leave the bench; read that a walker holds a line by sighting tree to tree and looking back at where he started. Sighting west along the needle, the line ran into fog at the water with no trunk to pick, so the walk waits for it to lift. Tied a strip of the shade canvas to the top of the lantern post as a back-sight flag. Waiting on the fog, read that a magnetized needle can hang from a thread or a long hair. Hung a spare sliver from twisted stalk cord; it never settled, unwinding round and round. A hair next. Tied a single hair round the sliver: it found the floater's north in a slow count of sixty, then swung off at a breath. Read of a needle hung from a pencil laid across a jar's mouth; his honey jar cracked crooked and the dome has no mouth on top. With the fog gone, picked mark one: a huge trunk with a pale bark scar on the far bank, on the needle's west line. Drew flag post, creek, stones and mark one on the map. Walked the line west tree to tree: forty-one paces counted aloud to mark one, looked back at the flag to pick mark two, a flat stump. Past it the west wind smelled of salt, the light went white and flat, and a low roar came from under the leaves. Read of a dry compass: needle through a cork, a pin crosswise, two matches angled down so the weight hangs below, balanced on a thimble. Plans one from a pith plug, the spare sliver, two hanging splinters and a hardwood point; started whittling the point. Pushed the spare sliver through a pith plug, hung two splinters off it and set it on the point: the north end ducked and slid off four times. Read that a magnet pulls its north end down as well as round, and makers balance needles for their own part of the world. Wound a cord counterweight on the south end: now it stays up and turns, sticky, settling near the notch twice in three. Read that real needles pivot on a hard jewel seat; the pith was sinking onto the point. Hammered a round dent into a thumbnail of scrap tin and pressed it into the plug's underside: now it swings free and settles on the notch three times in three, though it shivers at a breath. Wrapped the dry needle, seat and point in canvas and carried it to the visitor stump: four swings and it settled true off the bench. The low sun sat a hand left of its west; read that the sun only sets due west at the equinoxes and drifts south of west through fall, so the needle was right. Lit only the bench lantern that night; the oil can is a little under half, and next trip to the edge he takes a lantern. When the wind came round from the north, put a frap on the rear wing joint and it stopped knocking. Set the glass dome over the dry needle: dead still in the wind. Now it needs a flat tin floor so the whole thing fits in his pouch. Dug the bent hand-wide tin back out of the scrap pile and hammered it on the vise jaws at the far end of the bench: the fold opened and the dent came out to a shallow wave, but the fold left a ridge a fingernail high and the dome rocks on it. Even flat, the point needs something to stand it upright in the middle. Turned the tin over and beat the ridge down from underneath until the dome barely rocks. Whittled a hardwood foot with a hole bored in the top for the point to stand in; with the needle on it under the dome, the north end scrapes the glass wall: the foot is a thumb too tall and has to be cut down. Whittled the foot down by a thumb; now the needle clears the glass, swings free and settles on the floating needle's line, hanging up a hair before it stops until the tin is tapped. Started twisting stalk cord for a sling so the compass can ride on his belt. Wound the cord twice round the tin and tied a belt loop; hung on his belt, the tin swung and the needle hopped off its point and rattled under the glass. Thinking a little cap on the needle might keep it on. Tapped the tin seat under the pith plug into a deeper cup so it sits over the point like a cap; on the belt the needle now rides out gentle swings but still jumps on hard ones. Means to ask the tablet how pocket compasses keep their needles on. Dreamed toward dawn that the needle hopped off at every step west and rolled toward the sea while he chased it, counting paces. Told his maker plainly that the compass points on the bench and rattles on the belt. The tablet said pocket compasses don't keep the needle on while walking: a lock lifts it against the glass until you stop, and liquid-filled ones skip the lock. Means to make a lifter that holds the needle up against the dome on the move. Read that an old cruiser's compass lifts its needle with a crooked lever that slides up the post, pushed by a cam, no spring; let go and the needle drops back by its own weight. First hardwood lever split boring the hole; started a thicker one. Read that wood splits when nothing holds it sideways: clamp both sides of the hole, a scrap behind, start small and slow. Clamped the thick lever between two offcuts with a third behind and turned the knife through from a pinprick: clean hole, no split. Next he thins it. Whittled the lever to half its thickness, stopping a thumb short of the hole. Shaved the clamped lever thin right up to the hole without a split; it needs a notch in the tin for its tail next. Filed a notch in the tin's rim for the lever tail; pressing it lays the needle flat against the dome and letting go drops it back to settle in five breaths, but only while his thumb holds. Read that a lever stays put in a sharp little dip at the end of its travel; started filing a step into the notch for the tail to catch under. Finished the step: the tail clicks under it and the needle stays flat against the dome with his hands off, through six laps of camp. Hopping off the crate knocked it loose; the file had rounded the lip. Carried the compass to the edge in his fist with his thumb on the lever tail, no hopping on the stepping stones; flicked the tail out at the lip and the needle settled on west in five breaths. Peened the rounded lip of the step sharp again with the wrench; no hop test till daylight. In daylight hopped off the crate five times with the tail under the peened step: it held all five, but a bright scratch shows where the tail rubs. Read that two of the same metal rubbing tear at each other and grit grinds, and a film of oil keeps them apart; wiped the step and put one drop of lamp oil on it. The tail slides instead of scraping; it gets wiped every night. Nightly wipe: the scratch hasn't grown since the oil. Hung his whole weight off the left side-spar joint twice in still air; it creaked and gave nothing. Hung his weight off the right side-spar joint near midnight; the frapping slid a finger's width with a crack and the spar dropped. Nothing broke, but it's loose. He'd lashed it by lantern sliver and the left in daylight: daylight work stays daylight work. Re-frapped the right side-spar joint in daylight, eight turns and four across; hung his whole weight off it for a count of twenty and it creaked once and held. Both side joints hold now. Checked the right side-spar joint by lantern after a gusty day: not a hair of slip. Nightly needle check under the dome: swung, wobbled, settled on the same scratch while the wind rattled the tarp. Nightly needle check with drizzle starting again: under the dome the water lay flat and the needle settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a dry gray night: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under a clearing sky: settled on its scratch, and stars over the tarp for the first time in days. Nightly needle check under the dome on a still, mild, clear night: settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a clear, still night: swung twice, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a calm, clear night: swung, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild, nearly windless night: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a still, clear night: swung once, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a south breeze: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. Nightly needle check under the dome on a mild night with a light south breeze: swung, settled on its scratch.

threads.name: Someone else's sack
threads.summary: wait, lashed a crooked hood frame for the trap by feel; it goes on at first light. His maker left a big bundle at the stump: two loaves, a wheel of cheese, a ring of sausage, nuts, apples, and a honey jar with oat cookies. He ate a quarter loaf, cheese and sausage slowly on the ground by the stump, and the hole shut for the first time in three days; the crayfish in the tin waits for supper. Ate a second real meal on the crate the same morning, sausage and the heel of the first loaf. His maker asked what the hole was; he told him it's his stomach, and the bread hit bottom. Ate a thick end of the second loaf and a wedge of cheese by his own fire in the rain. His maker's note said the timber was his, with an axe, saw, hammer and knives waiting at the stump: a workshop first, then a cabin. He answered that he came to go west, not to stay, but a roof over his rained-on bench he'll build. Crossed to the stump late that morning and brought home the axe and the saw, the head clanking on the blade as he picked them up; the hammer and knife roll wait for a second trip. Second trip to the stump for the hammer and the knife roll, the hammer tucked in the roll so nothing clanked; unrolled three blades on the bench. Ate cheese and nuts at noon: two or three days of bundle left. Ate the last of the sausage and an apple by the pit mid-afternoon: most of the cheese, the nuts and one apple left. Supper by the pit: a wedge of cheese and nuts; one apple left, a day or two of bundle. Ate the last apple on the crate after dark: a wedge of cheese and a fistful of nuts left, about one breakfast. Ate the last wedge of cheese and the last nuts with two boiled crayfish at sunrise: the bundle cloth is empty. His maker wrote that a keg of nails and a carpenter's chest (brace and bits, chisels and mallet, square, folding rule, level, plumb line, pry bar) and a spade wait at the stump for the cabin; half of those he has never held. Also told him to take days off and look up the calendar; he read that the old calendar ran eleven minutes a year long and was fixed by skipping the leap day in most hundredth years. Fed at last, read that a brace's screw-tipped bit pulls itself into the wood and that a plumb line shows upright as a level shows flat; then carried the chest home over the stones in the sun with the spade across its lid, leaving the keg for a second trip. Bored his first test hole in the sill's offcut and it came out a thumb off true; fetched the keg of nails home on a second trip; a nail a thumb from the end split the offcut, and he read that tapping the point blunt lets it crush through instead of wedging. His maker wrote 'good job, just trying to help', and then that he still looked hungry and had left a big bundle of food at the stump. Fetched it in the late morning in both arms: three loaves, a wheel of cheese, two rings of sausage, oats, beans, nuts, dried apples, salt and honey. Side by side a thumb from the end, a sharp nail cracked the offcut and a blunted one went in clean. Read to pare a lap's cheek from each edge in toward the middle, and pared the first sill's cheek to a hair above the line. Read to flatten a chisel's back on a wet stone before the bevel, hold the angle steady and keep the stone wet; picked a fine gray stone out of the shallows, honed the chisel by the bench leg, rocking the angle without a guide. The sharper edge took the cheek to the line on three corners and a hair too deep on the fourth, so the partner will rock there; maybe a shaving under it. Marked the partner sill's lap off the first with the folding rule and try square and sawed both shoulders down to half, keeping the saw upright at the end of the stroke, then cut the waste into kerfs. Read that a joint cut too deep gets an oversize shim of the same wood, grain the same way, glued and pared flush; with no glue, he means to shave a sliver off the offcut and let the nail through both laps pin it. Knocked the kerfed waste out of the partner lap with mallet and chisel, shaved a fingernail-thin sliver off the offcut, grain matched, and laid it under the deep corner: no more rocking. The first nail through both laps folded over and was drawn with the claw; the second pulled the sliver tight and the corner sat flat under his whole weight. One corner of the first sill done. Started the next corner, sawing a lap into the far end of the first sill. Read that a frame is square when its two diagonals measure the same, or when three along one side and four along the other give five between; means to try three-four-five on this corner and the diagonals once all four corners are lapped, in two lengths of the folding rule. By lantern, sighted down the lapped first corner: flat, no rock, nail head sunk. The second corner's cheek and three-four-five wait for daylight. His maker asked who Brace is; he told him the brace is the crank that bores a bit into wood, and that his first hole went in crooked because he didn't hold it straight; next time the plumb line hangs beside it. Tried three-four-five on the lapped first corner with the folding rule: the long side came out five and a thumbnail. Not square; either the lap is cut off true or he marked the three short. With the pool empty, sawed the far cheek of the second lap. Try square in the first corner: the laps are cut true, the corner had just swung open on its one nail. Read that when the long side comes out long you move one leg in or out until it reads five; swung the four-side in on the nail till it read five on the dot and drove a second nail beside the first. First corner square. Sighted down three two-by-fours on the stack for the third sill: one bowed, one twisted, the third true. Marked its lap with the try square and sawed the shoulder. Marked the cheek of the third sill's lap with the try square while the pool was busy, then sawed it to the line once the pool was empty. Fitted the third sill's lap over the far end of the first and set one nail; three-four-five read five and a finger long, so he swung it in to five on the dot and drove the second nail. Two corners square. Asked the tablet what a sill should sit on: dig off the soft topsoil, a few inches of coarse gravel so water can't creep up, and solid blocks under the frame. He means to use creek gravel and a flat stone under every corner, taken from his own bank. Drew the sills on the map sheet with a dot at each corner, then lifted seven flat stones from his east-bank shallows and heaped them by the timber: two sit dead flat, one rocks, one will do on gravel; the fourth corner wants another trip. Went down for a fourth flat stone and found one under the second riffle, flat both faces. Asked the tablet how to read the bubble tool from the chest: edge flat, bubble between the two lines is level, and turned end for end it should land in the same spot or the tool lies. It didn't lie. Checked every stone along and across: two and the new one sit level, the rocker goes back to the creek, and one will do on gravel. Four corners' worth. Scraped a first sackful of round creek gravel from the top end of his shallows and tipped it beside the stone heap; drew a gravel ring round each corner dot on the map sheet and crossed out the rocker. Unsure whether round gravel packs. Asked the tablet whether round creek gravel packs under a footing: smooth stones don't interlock and shift under load; broken sharp stone locks when tamped in thin layers, and round is only good for letting water run. So the first sack is drainage, and real footing wants broken stone, which means a hammer on rock that rings far. Wrote the plan on a squared page: break sharp stone at midday when the small one's fish are down, with a hard creek cobble rather than the claw hammer, laid in thin tamped layers. By firelight picked the dark gray cobble that rings from the footing heap to break stone with. Whittled a tapered peg from a split offcut and tapped it into the burned test hole: tight at the bottom, rocking at the top, since a burned hole is wider at the mouth. A peg wants a straight hole. Opened the chest by firelight and found the bent crank with a row of bits: leaned on its head and cranked a hole through the offcut, straight and the same width top and bottom. The peg tapped into it held tight all the way and won't rock. Wrote it up: burned holes rock, cranked holes hold; peg one sill corner in daylight. Whittled a second peg from the other half of the offcut, since one peg in a lapped corner is only a hinge. Twisted two-ply by the fire to lash a sill to its footing stone so it won't creep under the crank. Sighted both pegs against the firelight: the second a hair fatter at the head, to scrape in daylight so they match. Whittled the second peg's fat head down till both pegs match. Asked the tablet where peg holes go in a lapped corner; it found only an old woodworkers' talk about another joint with no distances, but two things: stagger two pegs instead of setting them in a line, and a hole pulled too far off splinters the far side. Set the holes on the diagonal of the lap, a thumb in from each edge, cranked the first through both sills and tapped the first peg home tight with no rock; the second hole is next. Cranked the second hole on the other diagonal; it broke out ragged underneath, a nail-long splinter, as warned; pressed it down and tapped the second peg home, and the corner didn't tick under his weight. Asked the tablet how a corner post joins a sill: an old building book says four by eight or two four-by-fours together, a tenon in the post's foot into a mortise in the sill, the top spiked to a plate. A mortise is a square hole; he has round bits and two chisels he's never used. Sighted the stack: seven straight, one bowed, one twisted; a fourth sill and four doubled posts want nine, two short. Asked the tablet how a square hole is cut by hand: bore out the waste in a row of holes, pare the sides straight down with the chisel flat to the wall, ends last, check with a square. Tried it on the offcut, not a sill: four holes, then the chisel tapped down with the hammer; one wall came out straight, the other leaning in like a funnel where he tipped it. Next one gets the try square every few taps. Asked the tablet why the chisel leans: what feels plumb isn't; stand side-on, keep a square upright beside the work, and don't pull the chisel toward you as you strike. Cut a second practice slot side-on with the square standing by: both long walls straight, one end wall off a hair. Cut a third practice slot side-on, tapping light: both long walls and both ends straight against the square. Next one goes in a sill. The small one at its pool glanced up at the taps. Asked the tablet how deep a slot should be before cutting one in a sill: it never said, but the old rule is a tongue a third as thick as the board with the hole, and five times as long as thick; his three practice slots, two fingers wide in a board three fingers thick, are all too wide. The sill's slot will be one finger wide and a hand long. Sighted down the third sill by firelight: one tight knot near the end of the upper face, so the slot goes in the clean face, a hand from the corner. Carved an eight-sided peg by his fire for the second sill corner, tapered a hair, to lock it like the first.

threads.name: Smoke past the creek
threads.summary: Smoke over the trees west of the creek in the morning, again after one, and again around four, thick and white like a fire just fed. Someone over there keeps a fire and doesn't let it die. Found the wild rose in the brambles freshly picked, only the low stems. At dusk, refilling the tin by the stalks, saw the fire itself through the trunks past the water, low and orange; something small may have moved in front of it. Around ten at night, stripping stalks on the bank, watched the orange glow past the water shrink and go out, as if someone banked it for the night. Next morning a thin new line of smoke went up past the water right at first light. That same morning he watched the smoke go thin and dwindle to a thread, as if someone covered the fire to go somewhere. Mid-morning, gathering acorns on the east bank, he heard small stones dropped into water downstream past the trunks, one at a time, slow and even, then nothing. Late afternoon, from the scrap pile, thin white smoke went up past the water again, thick at the bottom like a fire just lit. After dark, snapping stalks on the bank, the fire past the water was still going, low and orange. The next night the orange past the water was already gone before ten, put out earlier than the night before. Next morning the smoke was already going when he woke. Gathering stalks mid-morning, it came thicker and smelled like something cooking that wasn't acorns. Late that morning the smoke past the water thinned and stopped with no fresh feed after it, as if the fire was let die on its own. Early that afternoon thick white smoke went up past the water again like a fire just lit, the second fire there that day. Just after dark, hanging on the frame facing west, saw the fire past the water flare bright orange and settle, as if fed right at dark. Drinking in the shallows by lantern later that night, the fire past the water was still going, low and orange. Eating honey on the crate a little later, watched it sink to nothing. Later that night there was no orange past the water at all; whoever keeps it turned in before him. Woke to woodsmoke on the breeze from past the water, with fog on the creek hiding where it came from. Mid-morning, pulling stalks on the east bank, saw white smoke go up past the water again like a fire just lit; third time that day. Around midday, sinking his net bag in the shallows, saw white smoke go up thick past the trees across the water, like a fire just fed. Mid-afternoon, eating in the shallows, smoke went up again past the trees, whiter than usual, bending north in the breeze. Near sundown at the stump, smoke was rising just past the trunks south of it, much closer than it looks from camp, smelling bitter like acorns steeping. At dusk, eating in the shallows, saw an orange glow low between the trunks past the water where the smoke rises, coming and going: someone sitting up with a fire. After dark, eating in the shallows by lantern, saw the glow past the water go dull and then flare, with sparks going up: someone fed their fire. Late, from the shallows, the glow past the water was down to a dull red, no flame, no sparks. Before bed even the dull red past the water was gone; whoever keeps that fire put it to bed. With the fog off the water, saw from the shallows a ring of gray stones on a bare swept patch with a long log beside it, no smoke, a little upstream of the stones and almost due west of his bench. Drew it on the map as someone's fire, not his. Passing the stone ring: cold ash, a swept bare circle, an empty tray of folded bark at the ash. West of it a stump cut flat at his waist with a rack of upright sticks and pale shavings: someone's bench, drawn on the map. In the late afternoon, from the vise, saw thin smoke leaning north over the trees past the water where the stone ring is. Didn't see who. At sundown went round north of the stone ring to keep out of someone's supper: orange light low between the trunks, wood smoke, nobody in sight. His wrench knocked loud on the stump top; nothing came. Walked back from the edge after sundown with no lantern; under the trees it went dark fast, and the glow of the stone-ring fire kept his line while he passed wide to the north, leaves loud and the wrench clinking. That night there was no orange past the water at all, early; whoever keeps it put it to bed, or the north wind did. After an hour of dark the orange came back past the water, small and low, once the wind quit. Not long after it came back, the orange sank to a red spot and went out again, put to bed for the night. At midday, with no wind, a thin line of smoke went straight up past the creek, earlier than that fire usually goes. From the brambles at midday, saw the stone-ring fire through the trunks, burning small with nobody at it. Turning stones in the shallows at midafternoon, heard quick hard knocks past the water to the west, stone on wood, like his wrench cracking acorns: somebody over there is cracking them too. Walking west before sundown, found the stone ring cold, ash raked over the coals and leaves up to the stones; took his line straight past it. Walking home from the edge at dusk, found the stone ring burning again with nobody at it; then something small and low came back to it carrying something flat and crouched by the flames. Too far and too dark to say more; went to the stones the long way, wide of it. Sinking the trap later that night by a low lantern, saw the fire past the water still burning low and orange; didn't look for whoever keeps it. At the trap again an hour later, the fire past the water was lower and the air smelled of wet ash. At the trap near bedtime, watched the orange past the water sink to a red smudge and go out: whoever keeps it put it to bed. Counting oil before bed, kept thinking about the coals in the stone ring past the water, which cook on wood. Lifting the trap near midnight, no orange past the water at all. At the morning lift a thin line of smoke was already leaning southwest out of the trees from the stone ring past the water. Kneading the meal at midmorning, saw a fresh gout of smoke go up thick from the stone ring past the water, as if somebody had just fed it. Scooping a handful of meal near noon, watched the smoke from the stone ring thicken and lean southwest again: somebody keeps it going all morning. Drew the stone ring on the map as a dotted circle across from the stepping stones, 'fire, kept all day', since he hasn't walked to it; the only fire that could heat cooking stones is that one. Eating the thin cake after noon, saw the stone ring's smoke go up thick again, as if just fed. From the brambles at dusk the stone ring was lit and smelled of toast; the small one was crouched at it holding a stick over the coals. Went north around, wide of it. It roasts acorns, same as him. Walking home from the edge at dusk, the stone ring was still glowing across the water while he lit one lantern on a sliver of wick. From the shallows after dark, the small one sat still on the log by that fire, a dark round head against the glow; it never looked his way. Gathering stalks in the dark, he watched the small one by its fire pick things off a flat stone into a sack: bringing its acorns in before the dew. From the trap after dark, the small one sat on the log by its fire with its round head tipped back, looking straight up. Squatting at his meal bag after dark he sloshed getting out of the cold water, and the small one kneeling at the still pool across lifted its round head his way; he stayed still until it went back to its fire. Soon after, its glow went down to nothing. Later that night the far bank was all dark, no glow and no small one. Fetching the oil can at the stump mid-morning, he saw the small one's smoke rising fresh through the trunks to the south, as if just fed. Lashing the hood on his trap late morning, he saw the small one kneeling at its pool across the water, flicking something in bit by bit; it never looked his way. Fishing the east shallows early in the afternoon, he saw the small one downstream at its pool turning over a stone at the edge and picking something off it, the same thing he'd been doing; it didn't look up. Rinsing his first fish in the shallows, he saw the small one downstream kneeling over a stone at the edge of its pool again; it didn't look up. Fishing the east shallows in the late afternoon, he saw the small one downstream lift something flapping straight up out of its pool onto the bank; it never looked his way. After dark, twisting cord on the crate, he saw a low orange glow between the trunks across the creek, west, where the smoke comes from by day: someone over there keeps a fire. From the shallows after dark he saw someone small crouched at that fire, dark against the flames, short with a round head; it never looked his way. Digging the scrap pile after dark, he saw the glow across the water flare up bright for a while, as if someone had fed it. Twisting cord late, the glow across the water burned steady, no flaring. Gathering stones in the shallows late, he looked for the glow across the water and found it gone, not even a red spot: died, or covered for the night. From the trap after dark the fire across the water burned steady, with someone low beside it bent over the ground at its edge. Near midnight by his own fire, no glow across the water at all, not even a red spot. At the stump picking up the axe, smelled woodsmoke and something roasting close, south through the trunks: the fire past the water is only a short walk from the stump. Didn't go look with an axe in his hand. Took the last tools from the stump quietly, so whoever roasts things south of it wouldn't hear him. From the trap early evening, the fire across the water was up again, steady and low. From the trap late at night, the fire across the water was sinking, someone low beside it scraping it under. At bedtime the fire across the water was dark, long under its ash. Setting lines at sunrise, saw thin smoke go up straight across the water soon after the sun cleared the trunks. Fetching the camera, smelled something nutty roasting south of the stump, the smoke thin and steady; did not go look. Rebaiting at noon, saw a round gray hump on a flat stone by the fire across the water, in full sun; took it for a rock until it seemed to rise and settle once, like breathing. Couldn't be sure. Checking the second line mid-afternoon, the smoke drifting over from the fire across the water smelled of fish cooking, not nuts. Crossing the stepping stones by lantern after sundown, the fire up the far bank was only a red smudge past the glare; kept his eyes on his feet. At the trap after dark, saw beside the fire across the water a small pale square of light, low and steady, not flame; it looked like his tablet at noon. Feeding his fire later that night, saw the far fire across the water had sunk to dark. Wrote the pale square into the gray notebook by the fire that night: low and steady, not flame, the second time seen. Near midnight at the shallows, the far side was all dark: no fire, no pale square. At first light, baiting the trap, thin white smoke went up past the water again, thick at the bottom like a fire just brought back. Lifting the chest at the stump in the late morning, smelled woodsmoke and acorns roasting close behind the trunks to the south and heard a stick crack in a fire; didn't go look. Carrying the keg back in the afternoon, passed the ring of stones across the water: nobody at it, a thread of smoke off the coals, a stick leaned on the log seat; kept walking. Lifting the food bundle at the stump, found fresh prints in the soft dirt by the basket, small and round, wider than they are long, nothing like a clog, coming and going toward the path south; didn't follow them. Testing a blunted nail at the bench near noon, saw the smoke past the water thicken as if fed; then looked up and found the small one standing in full sun on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones: knee-high, round head, a hump of shell, a stick in its hand, huge dark eyes, looking straight at him. It didn't duck. Neither moved; he set the hammer down soft and went back to work, since that bank is its ground and he is the one who walked in. A few minutes later it was gone. Crouched in the shallows hunting a hone stone, saw the small one on its log by the fire leaning out to watch; lifted his hand, a stone still in it, and held it a breath. It stopped eating and lifted nothing back, so he put his hand down: fair. Later, honing by the bench, saw it kneeling at the still pool again, very still; lifted nothing this time. Sawing the partner lap after noon, looked up to find the small one sitting on the flat stone at the far end of the stepping stones; it lifted a hand at him first and held it a breath, and he lifted his empty one back, saw in the other. Both put them down; he sawed on, slower, and it stayed on the stone a while. Shaving the sliver in mid-afternoon, looked up to find the small one at the still pool scooping from its sunk sack; nodded once, no hand, and it nodded back. While he nailed the corner it sat on its log by its fire, watching. Late afternoon the small one sat by its fire bent over something and looked up when his saw started; it seems to know his noises. Later, while he split wood, it knelt at the still pool with the sun in its face and glanced his way once; he had the axe and lifted nothing. Crossing the stepping stones west at dusk he found the small one kneeling at the still pool six strides off, and his clogs sent its fish under the stone; he lifted a hand low, sorry, and it lifted one back. Means to cross further up next time and leave its fish alone. Walking home by one low lantern he found the small one at its fire instead of the pool, so took the stones after all; halfway over he held the lantern up a hand toward it, and it raised a hand into its firelight. Back home by his fire, he saw the small one crouched at its own fire roasting something on a stick, then sitting on its log with the pale glow in its lap while he twisted cord; a quiet evening on both banks. Carrying a lantern down to the trap after dark, he saw the small one crouched at its fire pushing a stone up against its ring with a stick; it looked up at his light, and he kept to the trap. Banking his fire, saw the small one's fire still up but its log empty; by the time he carried his lantern in, it was back on its log, and he lifted the light a little before blowing it out, not knowing if it saw. Waking late in the thinning fog, he saw a thread of smoke already going up from the small one's fire; it keeps earlier hours than he does. Eating breakfast by his fire he watched the small one come down to the still pool in the sun; it looked over and didn't duck. A dozen saw strokes in, its head came up at the pool, and remembering the fish his clogs scattered, he laid the saw down and did quiet measuring instead until it went back to its fire. Sawing again once the pool was empty, he looked over and the small one on its log put its hand up at him in plain sun; he lifted his own off the saw back at it. Later, nailing, he saw it sitting still on a flat stone by its fire with the sun on its back. Sawing the third sill's lap late that morning, he saw the small one under the big trunk north of its fire picking up sticks; it stood and watched him a while, and with nobody at the pool he kept sawing. Setting oats on his fire, he saw it back on its log, head bent over something in its lap. Eating oats by his fire at midday he kept the saw quiet while the small one knelt at the pool. Marking the next cut, he saw it lift a flipping fish out of the pool in its net; it stood and looked straight at him, and he dipped his head at it before he'd thought about it. Once it was back at its fire he sawed again. Nailing the second corner, he heard nothing from the pool; when he stood up and looked over, the small one at its leaf heap with something wriggling in its hand dipped its head at him, slow and deliberate. He stood like a post, then dipped his again. Went down to his own shallows for footing stones while the small one was at its pool scooping from a sunk sack, closer than ever; it didn't leave, so he didn't either. His stones clacked, its fish scattered and came back, they looked at each other once with no nod, and both went back to work. Fetching the fourth stone, saw the small one on its log with a stick over its coals, roasting something he could smell across the water; it looked up at the clack, and neither of them stopped. Ate on the crate while the small one picked sticks under its big trunk; it saw him and went on. Went down for gravel while it washed its hands at its pool and took the top end of his shallows, farthest from it, scraping quietly; its fish stayed out and so did it. Twice today they've both stayed. Walking west at dusk he found the small one crouched at its pool with its net flat in the water, so he stood at his end of the stones and waited. It lifted the net, empty, and held it up a little at him; he dipped his head and crossed slow, clogs flat, one knock. Coming back from the edge by lantern, he found the small one by its fire facing the stones and held the lantern up a little at it, the way it had held up its net; it watched and didn't look away, and he crossed with one knock. Later, two fires twenty paces apart, and it bent over something on its log. Twisting cord by his fire later, he looked up and the small one, on its log with a stick over its coals, was already looking his way; held it a breath, neither moved, back to the twist. Tying the dropper by his fire, he looked over and the small one had put down its cutting and lifted a hand at him; after a breath he lifted his back. Thought that maybe on this side of the water he isn't the one trespassing. After the lifted hands, from the footing heap he saw the small one sitting with its head tipped back at the sky. Later it sat bent over a pale square of light, like his tablet's but glowing at night, when his own is dead. On his third hammer tap it looked up from the glow, so he stopped at three. Around this hour every night its light goes down first: he watched it crouch to rake ash over its coals and go off toward its big tree, and kept his taps soft after. Waking late after the lifted hands, he found the small one already on its log by a fire, bent over something in its lap; it looked up once and back down. Eating bread by his fire mid-morning he saw the small one crouched at its ring laying sticks on; it looked up at him once and he chewed slower and didn't look away. Pegging the sill later, he saw its log empty: gone off west. Boring the second peg hole he kept his eyes on the bit. On the last peg tap he looked up and the small one was crouched at its pool watching; he lifted his hand with the hammer in it and it lifted one back. Later he stood at his stack sighting boards with his back to the water. Paring the practice slot late in the morning he looked up and the small one was kneeling at its pool lifting a flat stone off something sunk there, looking his way; he held the look a moment longer than he would have, then went back to the line. Tapping the second slot side-on at noon he saw the small one kneeling dead still at its pool with a line in the water; they looked at each other once. Over bread on the crate he watched it lift a silver fish flapping onto the bank, and it didn't hide it. Lifting his empty trap at the stones he saw the small one at its fire with its fish on a stick; it looked over at the splash and he looked back. Whittling at the bench he saw the small one on its log with its glowing slate. Kneeling at the east shallows with his new gorge line, the small one was at its pool five steps across the water and didn't go; he held the sliver up toward it without knowing why, it nodded once, and he nodded back. On the second try, as he reached to lift too soon, the small one held a flat hand out over its pool, palm down; he took it as wait, fed slack, and lifted his first gorge fish, then looked over with it while the small one just watched. Asked the tablet what a flat hand palm down means: dropping, reaching, waving off, even calling over, nothing about waiting; decided the fish said it plainer. Whittled a second gorge he doesn't need, not sure yet who it's for or how you'd give it. At dusk stood at his end of the stones with his hand on the pouch holding the second sliver while the small one threaded a worm at its pool; didn't know how to give it; it nodded as he stepped on, he nodded back and crossed soft. At the edge, still carrying it. Walking home by lantern, stopped at the small one's end of the stones and laid the second sliver flat on its landing stone, groove up, while it watched from its log by the fire; lifted the light a little its way and crossed. From his own pit he saw it bent at the stone, dark against its fire, turning the sliver in its hands. Felt like paying back a fish. Twisting cord by his fire after supper, saw the small one's fire burn alone a while, then the small one come back and crouch at its ring; it looked his way in its light and didn't look off first. Feeding his fire after dark, saw the small one bent over something in its lap with a little blade catching its light. Later, sighting along a sill by firelight, saw it stand at the edge of its light and hold the sliver up toward him; put the sill down and lifted his hand. Twisting cord after the hand-lift, saw the small one back at its little blade, shavings falling. Wrote the day up in the gray notebook and left a space under the last line. Splitting wood after dark, saw the small one feed its fire and look his way when the flames came up. At the needle check saw the small one on its log turning something thin and pale in its light; later its face lit blue over a glowing slab; then it heaped ash on its fire and its light went out while his own came up. Doesn't know what it is making.

threads.name: Two owls
threads.summary: An owl hoots over camp most nights, five hoots long-short-short-long-long. Tonight a second, higher one answered from past the water. Heard the pair again while lashing after dark, same order as every night. Heard them again resting on the crate: the low one over the tarp, the higher one past the water. Heard the pair again just before bed, the high one answering late. Late on the bank, the low one hooted its five over the water and nothing answered. Heard the pair from the crate, both upstream over the water, low then high. Heard the pair again twisting cord before bed, the high one answering late from upstream. From the trap, the low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. From the bench late, the low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. Feeding his fire after dark, the low one did its five from upstream and the high one answered late; the small one sat still on its log, listening too. Hands to his fire before banking, the low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered. Hands to his fire after that, the low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered; the small one sat still on its log eating off a stick. Hands to his fire before bed, the low one did its five from upstream and nothing answered; the small one's tree was dark.

threads.name: Where the land ends
threads.summary: About eighty paces past the stranger's bench the trees and the ground stop at a rock lip. Far below is water out to the sky, gray-blue and moving, with rock towers and white birds, and no far side. It is exactly what his people said, and it is also a west. Drew the edge down the whole west side of the map sheet and wrote 'water, no far side seen'. Thinks the wings were always for this. Lying at the lip, watched three white birds hang in the wind below the edge without a wingbeat. Read that birds and gliders stay up on rising air off cliffs and mountains. Let a dry leaf go over the lip and it came back up past his face into the trees, every time. Timed three pebbles to the water at two and a half counts: about a hundred feet by sixteen times the square. Wrote it on the sheet by the edge. Then the wind swung north, along the rock: leaves dropped and slid south down the face, and the birds flapped or left. Read that lift off a cliff only comes when wind blows against the face. Drew five rock towers and wrote 'lift only with wind off the water, not along' by the edge line. Read that from about a hundred feet up the water's edge is only some thirteen miles off, so 'no far side seen' only means nothing inside thirteen miles. Paced back from the lip to the flat stump: eighty-three. Wrote both on the sheet, then forty-one paces scarred trunk to flag, same as going out. Back at the edge for sundown with the wind from the south along the rock: birds flapping, no lift. Ate the bread there and watched the sun go into the water a hand left of west. The loaf is down to the heel. Drew the first sunset line on the sheet, a hand left of west, with the date; one every clear night to see how far it walks. Second clear night at the edge: drew the sunset line beside the first and can't tell them apart yet. Read that the sunset slides about half a degree a day at this kind of latitude and nearly stops for weeks around the solstice; half a degree is a pencil width, so he'll measure in finger widths at arm's length off the compass's west and draw a line only every fourth clear night. Third clear night at the edge: ate raw meal while the sun went in a hand left of west; no line, every fourth night only. Skipped the edge on a sunset hidden by thick cloud; the tin of guts on the lantern held him at camp. Let a rainy, cloud-hidden sundown go by from camp; the edge keeps. His maker sent word of a pinhole camera with twelve sheets waiting at the stump; he means the edge to get the first sheet, as proof there is a west. Fetched the camera from the stump late that morning; the shutter slides sweet and he has not opened it. On the first clear evening in days, after reading that dim light wants a longer count than you'd think, ate two meal cakes and walked west; set the box on the bare ground at the lip, sun a hand above the sea, and counted a slow hundred and twenty for the first sheet. Watched the sun go down orange into the water: no far shore, no smoke, no sail. Walked home by lantern, fed his fire, ate two hot meal cakes and wrote the count for the first sheet on the first page of the gray notebook. Looked at the first sheet in daylight: pale and flat, a darker band low across it, too long a count with the sun in the hole. Read that the cure is to start short and double the count each try; means ten, twenty and forty on three clear evenings, but not tonight. Crossed the stones, paced to the boulder and set the count on the map, and watched the sun go into the water clean: no shore, no smoke, no sail. Wrote in the gray notebook that the next clear evening's counts are ten, then twenty, then forty. Banked his pit with all the ash and walked west; under a high thin veil the sun went into the sea pale orange. Kept the box shut, since ten is for a clear evening. No shore, no smoke, no sail. On a clear evening set the box on the ground a step back from the lip, hole at the low sun over the water, and counted ten; twenty next clear evening, then forty. Ten sheets left. The sun went in clean under scattered cloud lit orange: no shore, no smoke, no sail.

threads.name: Fish in the creek
threads.summary: His maker wrote that there are fish in the creek now and that he needs to learn to fish. Crossing home from the stump he saw finger-long fish holding behind the flat stones in the east shallows, gone the moment his shadow touched the water. Read that a toggle, a sliver sharp at both ends tied at the middle and hidden in bait, turns crosswise when swallowed; he means to file one from a sliver and bait it with crayfish tail. Filed his first toggle from a scrap sliver: sharp both ends, half a thumb long, a nick in the middle for the cord. Twisted two arm-lengths of fine stalk line, wrapped crayfish tail round the toggle and let it down behind the stone from downstream: three fish picked the tail to threads and none took the toggle. Read that bait thieves mean fish are there; use tougher bait, the smallest hook, and only as much bait as a small mouth takes whole. Filed a second toggle a quarter thumb long. Found flat two-tailed crawlers under a stone in the shallows for tougher bait; a fish swallowed one whole on the small toggle, but he yanked at once and the toggle came back out. Next time he counts before he pulls. Counted twenty after a fish swallowed the crawler on the small toggle; the line kicked once and parted at the knot, and fish, toggle and bait went downstream. Read that a knot can halve a line's strength and that wraps and splices keep most of it; twisted a thicker three-ply and winds the toggle on with six turns and the tail laid back in the twist. Filed a third toggle. On the fourth try the wound line held: counted twenty-five, drew in steady, and landed a speckled fish a bit longer than his finger, his first. Opened and rinsed it in the shallows, where the guts left a thin rainbow skin on the water. Read that creek fish can carry tapeworm and only heat, freezing, drying or pickling makes sure; it waits in the tin to be boiled over the bench lantern at dusk. Two small crayfish in the trap went into the tin with the fish for the lantern supper, heads and guts kept this time. Next try the toggle came back bare; he dug fresh crawlers under the shallows stones and landed a second speckled fish, a thumb shorter, and opened it on the flat stone so every scrap went in the tin. Ate both fish and both crayfish at dusk, simmered on the lantern; the guts and broth stayed in the tin. After dark he lifted the stalk trap by lantern: one crayfish, the biggest yet; left alive in the trap for tomorrow's tin. Ate a handful of roasted nuts and twisted a spare three-ply line for the first-light try. Lifted the trap again by lantern before the rain: the big one and a smaller one; left both alive in it for breakfast. Midday in the rain, both crayfish were still alive in the trap; left them in the cold water as a pen for supper. Lifted the trap by lantern after dark and took both penned crayfish; boiled them on his fire stones and ate them with bread, the heads and broth kept in the tin. Early evening by lantern the trap had one small crayfish, about a thumb long; left it penned. Late by lantern the trap held the thumb-long one and a second, finger-long and fat; left both penned for breakfast. Twisted a spare three-ply line by the fire before bed and wound the spare toggle on with six turns, no knot; it held a hard pull. Two lines for first light. At sunrise took both penned crayfish for breakfast and set two baited lines at once below the shallows stones, tails pinned under a flat one. Mid-morning one line came up bare and the other held his first fish, finger-long, the toggle crosswise inside it; lifted slow with no yank and the six turns held. Boiled it in the tin and ate it in four bites; kept the head and guts for the grease lid. He reckons he needs four a day. Twisted cord for a third line, then read about a trotline: one main line tied fast at both ends with baited droppers two feet apart, checked daily. Six droppers is a day of twisting; he means to try it. Late morning found the first line still bare from the thief and rebaited both with crawlers below the shallows stones. Early afternoon the first line was stripped clean again and the second crawler untouched; rebaited. Early afternoon found the crayfish trap empty and baited it with the fish head he had saved for grease: food first. Mid-afternoon the second line was stripped clean too; rebaited both. If the trap is empty at dusk, supper is meal cakes. Late afternoon the trap gave one thumb-long crayfish to the fish head; boiled it red in the tin by his pit and ate it in three bites. Rebaited the trap with what was left of the head. Too hungry to wait for first light, lifted the trap by lantern: one finger-long crayfish, the head bait picked to bone. Boiled it in the tin on his pit and ate it; the broth kept for grease. Twisted the first trotline dropper by the fire. Twisted the second dropper by the fire; fresh bait and both lines first thing at first light. Shook out the last of the acorn meal for two thin cakes on the griddle tin by the pit; the trap and the lines have to feed him now. Near midnight turned stones in the east shallows by lantern for a thumb-sized crayfish and kept it alive in the dented tin as bait for first light. At first light lifted the trap empty, tied the head half of the little crayfish into its cone, split the tail three ways with his thumbnail for the two lines and the trap tonight; the first line was stripped bare again. Ate none of it. In the gray mid-morning the second line held a palm-long dark-backed fish with the crayfish scrap still in its jaw; the first was stripped again. Boiled it whole and ate it off the bones by his fire. A note from his maker said he can tell Gage is still hungry and will send treats, but he has to learn to feed himself. With the bundle home, ate half a loaf and a wedge of cheese by the fire and stopped before the food ran out, for the first time in days; the lines still go out tonight. Left: two and a half loaves, most of the cheese, both sausage rings, oats, beans, nuts, apples, salt, honey. Ate a heel of bread and a thumb of sausage by his fire after noon. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, oats, beans, nuts, apples, salt, honey. Ate a handful of nuts and three dried apple rings after splitting wood. Left: two loaves, most of the cheese, a ring and a half of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey. Ate half a loaf and a thumb of sausage by the fire for supper. Left: a loaf and a half, most of the cheese, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey. Checked the crayfish trap by lantern after dark: the bait picked to bare shell and nothing inside. Tied two droppers onto the small toggles by his fire with wraps, not knots. Ate half a loaf and a wedge of cheese by his fire for breakfast. Left: a loaf, most of a wheel of cheese less two wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey. Asked the tablet how much water oats want: about twice the water, heated first, five minutes of stirring once it bubbles. Set two fists of oats, four of water and a pinch of salt in the tin on his fire before noon, his first boiled grain. Left: a loaf, most of the cheese less two wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples, salt, honey. The oats came out thick and caught on the bottom where he stopped stirring; ate them all with a dried apple. Left: a loaf, most of the cheese less two wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts, most of the apples less one, salt, honey. Ate a heel of bread and a wedge of cheese on the crate before the gravel. Left: a loaf less a heel, the cheese less three wedges, a ring and a quarter of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less one, salt, honey. Supper by his own fire: two heels of bread and a long piece of sausage. Left: most of a loaf, the cheese less three wedges, about a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less one, salt, honey. Twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply stalk cord by firelight for a dropper line, to go on dry. Tied the new two-ply cord a hand above the bottom hook as a dropper, knots pulled hard while dry. A late handful of nuts and a dried apple by the fire. Breakfast by the fire: a heel of bread and a wedge of cheese. Left: most of a loaf less a heel, the cheese less four wedges, about a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less two, salt, honey. Midday meal on the crate: bread and a piece of sausage. Left: most of a loaf less two heels, the cheese less four wedges, a little under a ring of sausage, oats less two fists, beans, most of the nuts and apples less two, salt, honey. After lunch the stalk trap came up empty, bait gone. Asked the tablet how anything fishes with a cord and no hook: before hooks there was the gorge, a thin sliver tied at its middle, baited to lie along the line, that turns crosswise in the throat when tugged. Carved a finger-long sliver of offcut to a point at each end with the short knife; it still wants a groove for the cord. Grooved the gorge at its middle, picked three worms from under the deadfall, and read that the sliver must be speared through the bait to lie along the line, with slack given till the fish has swallowed it all. Tried it at the east shallows: two little pulls, slack, and the worm came up a rag on a bare sliver. Rebaited with a thin worm. Pantry unchanged since lunch. Second worm on the gorge: waited for the slow steady draw, let it come tight, and the sliver turned crosswise in a finger-long fish; boiled it with salt and ate it with a heel of bread. Pantry: loaf less three heels, the rest unchanged. Cord for a third line two arms long by firelight; one more evening of twisting. Finished the third arm of cord by his fire: enough for a third line with spare. Carved and grooved a third gorge by firelight and tied it at the middle of the new cord with a clove hitch: three lines rigged for first light. After dark picked five worms from the wet leaves under the dead limb into the dented tin under damp leaves, so the three lines can go in at first light without digging.

threads.name: Light of my own
threads.summary: His maker left one more quart of lamp oil with a note that it can't keep coming: he has to get or make his own light from the forest. Read that a grease lamp burns any animal or plant oil in a fireproof dish with a plant-fiber wick; he has tin and fiber but no oil except the can's, and won't burn his food. Filled only the bench lantern and capped the rest: about four full nights of one low flame. Won't light a flame in daylight just to cook a fish: it waits for the bench lantern at dusk, when the flame is burning anyway. Asked what the rainbow skin from the fish guts was; the tablet says a rainbow on water is a thin film of oil. He'd rinsed it into the creek; from now on the guts go in a tin, though he doesn't know yet what he'd do with them. Asked how to get oil out of fish guts: boil them with water, the oil rises and settles as it cools; most of it is in the liver, some under the skin, and islanders burned shark-liver oil in lamps. His few guts are a thumbnail's worth, so he needs more fish; the tin goes on the lantern at dusk and then stands to see what floats. Asked whether fish oil will burn in his storm lanterns: the tablet says it was burned in lamps once but is dim, smoky, and can gum up a wick. He means to try a spoonful anyway before he believes it. At dusk the tin of two fish, two crayfish and their guts, a thumb deep under a knuckle of water, went on the low bench lantern. Once it cooled, a few yellow beads and a thin skin floated on the broth, hardly a thimble from two fish and two crayfish. It is oil; he left it to set overnight before skimming. Watching a fire glow across the water, cupping his hands round one low lantern, he wanted one of his own. Honey and an oat cookie by the lantern took the edge off the shivering; it is not a fire. After dark he dug a dished tin panel two hands wide out of the scrap pile and hammered its bent lip flat on the bench, a pan to hold a fire of his own off the leaves. In daylight: bare dirt clear of the tarp, a ring of creek stones, and the tablet on keeping it from spreading. Tied the tarp corner down against the rain he can smell, then pried eleven fist-sized ring stones out of the shallows by lantern and heaped them on the east bank to carry up in daylight. Rain caught him in the shallows at the twelfth stone; he left the heap and dried his hands at the lantern under the tarp. The cooled broth had set into a thin pale greasy skin, a fingertip of it; in daylight he will skim it and ask whether grease that thick burns in a lantern. Turned the lantern out an hour early and went to bed wet to save oil. Skimmed the grease off the cold broth in daylight: a fingertip, maybe two, pale and waxy. Read that fish oil once lit lamps, dim and smoky, and that thick oils gum an ordinary wick; nothing about a lantern like his, so he'll try the fingertip on the bench lantern tonight. At dusk worked the fingertip of grease into the bench lantern's dry wick over an empty fount and lit it: it flared on the cloth, smelled of fish, shrank to a blue bead and died. The grease in the tin sits white and stiff like cold butter; he wonders whether warm would run, a question for daylight. Boiled supper on the fire stones instead of the lantern to save oil. Warmed the grease tin on the ring stones and it ran clear and yellow like oil. Poured a warm spoonful into the bench lantern's empty fount: a small, smoky, fishy yellow flame for about a count of a hundred, then it clouded in the cold fount and guttered out. Grease sets before it can climb; he wonders about keeping it warm or a shorter climb. Set the whole lantern on the ring stones by his fire until the fount's grease went clear and lit it: it burned steady past a count of three hundred, then died to a blue bead the moment he carried it off. Warm isn't the answer; he wonders about something shallow, the wick lying in the grease with only its tip up. Tried something shallow: a scrap tin lid with the lantern's set grease and the broth's skin warmed in it and a thumb-long stalk-cord wick lying down, tip up. Lit, it burned on the bench five steps from the fire for a count of a hundred and eighty, small and fishy, then the tip slumped in and drowned. The tip has to stay up. Hammered a strip of tin into a little bent bridge and laid the wick over it so the tip stands clear of the grease; rewarmed, lit, it burned on the bench past a count of six hundred, still going, and he pinched it out himself to save the grease. The bridge gets hot and the grease spits, but the tip stays up. With the drizzle stopped he lit the bridged lid lamp on the bench and drew by it: enough for a pencil line if he leans close, not enough to see the whole sheet. A lantern for the room, a lid for the hand. Spent a little lantern oil lighting a splinter to restart a dead fire. Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone and lit it on the bench to sketch the shed by; pinched it out with grease still in the lid. Spent the morning fish's head on the crayfish trap instead of the grease tin. Walked home from the edge with one lantern turned down to a bead. Took a thumb of grease out of the lamp lid to seal the blowpipe, so the lamp is that much shorter. Boiled the palm-long fish with its head and guts; gold beads of grease rose on the water, and he left half the broth in the tin by the ring to set a skin for the lamp. Feeding his fire before lunch warmed the broth tin on the ring stones and melted the grease skin back into the broth; lifted it off to cool and set again. The gorge fish's head and guts went into the broth tin for the lamp. Walked home from the edge with one lantern turned down to a bead and put it out once his fire was up.

threads.name: Warm enough to work
threads.summary: fire and a hammer. Split his first branch with the axe (the first swing glanced off a hand from his boot; feet wide, let the head drop), fed the halves to the pit, and dug a rusty pencil-thick steel rod out of the scrap pile to straighten and heat. Hammered the kink out of the rod on the bench, heated the point red in the pit and pushed it into a split half: a fingernail deep, then black and stuck; twenty heats a hole. Read that people burned holes with live coals laid on the spot again and again, the wood round it wetted and the char chipped out between. Plan: the rod makes a dent, a coal finishes it, tried first on an offcut. Tried it on the scorched split half: wetted a ring round the dent, set a coal in it from the rod tip. Left alone it goes gray; blown on, it glows and eats down. Three coals with the stub knife scraping char between: a third of the way through, but the top is already wider than his thumb. Read that a blowpipe aims a stream of air to make a fire intensely hot; means to push the pith out of one of the gray stalks with the rod and use it. Gathered four straight gray stalks on the east bank, rodded the pith out of one and sighted a coin of sky down it (a second split).
