Blown through, it turns a coal near white and it eats fast; blown hard it whistles and throws ash in his eyes, but short soft breaths burn the hole a nail deeper and straighter, nearly halfway. After dark, short soft breaths down the stalk: no whistle, no ash, and the hole went past halfway by firelight. The top is still too wide for a snug peg. Fed the pit three split sticks and burned the hole clean through the split half by firelight: straight below, a finger too wide at the top. Whittled two pegs with the long knife on the crate; the first was too skinny at the tip, the fatter second wedges tight halfway, not driven yet. By the lit grease lamp sketched the shed three paces by two on the map sheet: sill boards lapped at the corners, corner posts, a top plate, braces; counted twenty-odd peg holes, and one hole took an evening, so burning them all is no plan. Whittled a second long-tapered peg by the pit; it wedges a hair deeper than the first. Two pegs, one hole; wants a faster way to bore. Carved a starter pit for the next hole with the stub knife and it ran along the grain into a slot as long as his thumb; across the grain it bites and stops. Cut the next starter pit across the grain by the grease lamp: the stub knife bit a round seat the size of a pea and stopped, no slot. Whittled a third peg by the fire late and shaved one side too far: lopsided, kept as a spare; shave all round next time. Fed the pit one thick stick before bed on the first clear night in days; the smoke went straight up. Woke to a gray pit and spent a little lantern oil on a splinter to relight it. Asked the tablet how to join boards with no nails or drill: every joint wants glue, screws or a power drill, even the laps get nailed; decided on lapped corners with one peg each instead of twenty-odd holes. Carried the first two-by-four from the stack to the bench in daylight and penciled a lap on one end. Bore down on the saw and the first cut wandered a pencil-width off and leaned a finger out of true. Read to cut on the waste side, start short strokes against a knuckle, forefinger down the handle, no weight; the second cut ran straight. Read that the long cheek of a lap is sawn on the waste side of the half-depth line and pared down to it after, edges toward the middle; sawed it with the sill on end in the vise and the waste dropped clean, leaving a low hump to pare with the long knife. Asked how to make a peg hole with no drill: a nail, a bow drill, a brace and bit, or a sharpened rod heated red-hot that burns through; means to try a rod from the scrap pile in his pit. His maker left him a notebook with squared pages; he fetched it from the stump and put the timber counts on the first page. Heated a pencil-thick rod from the scrap pile red in his pit and burned a peg hole into the offcut: a knuckle deep after three trips, ragged and funnel-shaped. Read that hot coals left on the spot, with the char scraped out and the wood wet around it, do better; means to try that. Wet the offcut round the hole and tried coals in it: each went gray unless he blew on it, and three coals with the char scraped out took the hole half a knuckle deeper with straighter walls. Read that a hollow stem steers a coal burn; the dead stalks are pith, so he is looking for something with a hole down the middle. Read that flute makers get a tube by splitting the wood, gouging the middle out and joining the halves again; means to split a dead stalk with the stub knife, gouge the pith with the hooked one and lash it back as a blowpipe. By firelight split a dead stalk with the stub knife, scraped the pith out with the hooked one (one thin end cracked, so both halves went a finger shorter) and lashed it back with cord. Blowing through it, the seam whistles, but pinched shut it turns a single coal from red to white; means to seal the seam with grease. Worked a little cold fish grease from the lamp lid into a length of cord and wound it over the seam: no more whistle, and a coal went from red to white in four slow breaths instead of ten, though the mouth end tastes of fish. Came back from the creek with stiff fingers and fed two sticks on before bed; the woodpile is down to about six sticks. With the woodpile at six sticks and the pit gone cold, chopped dry middles from the big dead limb, lit a splinter at a lantern for a thimble of oil and brought the fire back with two puffs of the pipe. Fed two dry middles onto red embers before eating; they caught without smoke. Woodpile down to four old sticks and the rest of the middles. Split an armful of dry middles out of the big dead limb in the late sun and hung the axe back on its loop; woodpile back up for the night. Came home from the edge to a cold pit, lit a splinter at the lantern for a thimble of oil and brought the fire back on shavings and two dry middles. Fed two dry middles crosswise onto the coals later in the evening; they caught without a puff. Woodpile: four old sticks and about half the armful of middles. Too tired to saw, banked the pit instead of feeding it: raked ash over the last coals and pushed the ring stones in, to see if a coal keeps till morning and saves a thimble of oil. Next morning, raked the banked ash open: one coal the size of a pea had kept near the bottom, and shavings and one puff of the pipe brought the fire back without a thimble of oil. Means to bank it deeper tonight. Asked the tablet how deep the ash goes to keep coals overnight: no number, just burn down to coals, set the half-burned sticks aside, and heap all the ash you have over them; depth is trial and error. Tonight it gets all the ash. Before noon the pit was down to embers; two dry middles laid on caught without smoke. Banked the pit under every bit of ash before the evening walk west, to see if a coal keeps till he's back. Back from the edge an hour after banking, two coals were still red under all the ash; shavings, two middles and one puff brought it up, and the lantern went down to a bead. Fed one split middle after dark and it took without smoke; firelight to bore and write by, no oil. Before bed set the half-burned sticks aside and heaped every bit of ash over the coals again, ring stones pushed in. Next morning one coal like a bead lay under the heaped ash; shavings, a half-burned stick and a long breath brought it up, a second dawn without oil. Mid-afternoon the pit was two red coals under gray; shavings, a split middle and a long breath stood it up without smoke. Before the edge, heaped every bit of ash over the coals again and pushed the ring stones in. Back from the edge after dark, one coal under the heaped ash again; shavings, a long breath and a split middle stood it up, and he ate supper by it with the lantern out. Fed one split middle after dark and it caught without smoke. Split six dry middles off the dead limb after dark so the dawn fire needs no oil. Fed one split middle at bedtime hours; it went up clean.

timber.note: nine two-by-fours left on the stack (seven straight, one bowed, one twisted), sixteen planks untouched; on the bench three sills lapped into two square corners, each held with two nails, the first corner now also locked with two staggered pegs in cranked holes on the diagonal of the lap (the second hole splintered out underneath and was pressed back); a fourth sill and four doubled corner posts would want nine straight boards; the offcut has test holes, nails and now a practice mortise slot two fingers by four, one long wall leaning in at the bottom, and beside it a second slot cut side-on with both long walls straight and one end wall a hair off; tool chest, spade and nail keg beside the lean-to; a gray hone stone by the bench leg; eight flat creek stones in the footing heap, four checked level for the corners; the dark gray ringing cobble set aside for breaking stone

woodpile: three old sticks and a few fresh-split dry middles, less five laid on the fire after dark and one split middle on the mid-afternoon fire; one half-burned stick by the pit, less one split middle to relight it after dark, less one more split middle fed after dark; plus six fresh-split dry middles off the dead limb after dark
